newsitem.title: UK: European oil traders say no progress on Iraq deals.
newsitem.headline: European oil traders say no progress on Iraq deals.

text.p: European oil traders said on Wednesday that they had made little progress towards securing contracts to lift Iraqi crude under the second six-month term of the United Nations oil-for-food programme.
"Have we made any progress?..The answer is no. (The Iraqis) are not yet ready to get things moving" said one major European refiner.
Iraqi Ambassador to the U.N. Nizar Hamdoon said on Wednesday that the $2-billion of oil sales would not resume until a new aid distribution plan is in place.
The fact no oil sales contracts will be submitted for U.N. approval before a distribution plan is likely to mean no Iraqi liftings will take place in June, Hamdoon said.
Traders confirmed that they are not expecting to lift cargoes from the Turkish port of Ceyhan on the Mediterranean before July.
They said the main sticking point on contract negotiations appeared to be a new pricing structure.
"The pricing structure is the key...that is the main subject that is blocking it," said one dealer.
Baghdad is expected to wait until the aid plan is in place before it submits a pricing formula for U.N. approval.
And sales will not resume until the pricing formula is in place.
"The pricing formula is needed for new contracts. There will be no oil lifted until then," said Hamdoon.

Some European traders have asked Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for the price formula for Kirkuk crude loaded at Ceyhan to take account of higher freight costs of 25-30 cents a barrel for shipping the barrels to destinations in northern Europe.
But they said that so far they have received no response from SOMO.
Traders are also uncertain whether they will have to make the long road trip to Baghdad to renew contracts.

"There is a lot of confusion. We do not know whether we will have to go (to Baghdad), or can also sign the contract by telex," said a trader for a European refiner which lifted oil under the first six-month programme.
Traders said the uncertainty gave the impression that SOMO was in no hurry to resume sales.
"They want put the brakes on. They still have money that has not been spent from the first round... The delays are on their side," a trader said.
Traders said that slow progress could push exports of Kirkuk and Basrah, loaded from the Gulf terminal of Mina al-Bakr, as high as one million barrels per day (bpd) in July and August.
Sales averaged 660,000 bpd in the first export wave which began in mid-December.
The deal was renewed last week and took effect on June 8.
Hamdoon reiterated on Wednesday that oil companies holding term contracts with SOMO would have their deals renewed under the second round of accord.
